title: Judge Likely to Miss Wild Card Series Due to Calf Injury, MLB Confirms
body:
Aaron Judge’s calf injury has become a looming headache for the New York Yankees as they head into the American League Wild‑Card Series, with manager Aaron Boone confirming the team is planning for the slugger to sit out the matchup against the Boston Red Sox. The 30‑year‑old outfielder, who has been a cornerstone of New York’s offense this season, was placed on the 10‑day injured list earlier this week after being diagnosed with a moderate strain in his right calf. Boone’s remarks on Tuesday left little doubt that the Yankees will have to navigate the postseason without their most potent bat.

The timing could not be worse for a Yankees squad that has relied heavily on Judge’s power and presence in the lineup. Over the course of the regular season, Judge has posted a .274 batting average with 38 home runs and 108 RBIs, numbers that placed him among the league’s elite power hitters and helped New York secure a postseason berth. His ability to drive in runs and change the complexion of games with a single swing has been a defining factor for a team that struggled with consistency throughout the year. Without him, the Yankees must turn to a deeper bench and rely on younger players to fill the void.

Boone’s decision to essentially bench Judge reflects both medical caution and strategic pragmatism. A moderate calf strain, while not career‑threatening, can linger and worsen if a player is rushed back too quickly, especially in the high‑intensity environment of playoff baseball. The Yankees’ medical staff likely evaluated the risk of aggravating the injury against the potential upside of having Judge in the lineup. Given that the series is a best‑of‑three format, there is little margin for error, and a compromised player could become a liability. By opting to sit Judge, the organization hopes to preserve his health for a possible deeper run should they advance.

The absence of Judge forces the Yankees to lean on other offensive contributors. Outfielder Alex Verdugo, who has been a steady presence in the middle of the order, will likely see an uptick in clutch situations, while first‑base prospect Anthony Rizzo, returning from his own injury layoff, could be tasked with providing the power that Judge normally supplies. Additionally, the team’s bench depth—players like Gleyber Torres and Jasson Dominguez—may see expanded roles. The bullpen, which has been a point of concern all season, will also be under pressure to keep games close, allowing the offense to stay within striking distance even without a guaranteed home‑run threat.

Boston, meanwhile, stands to benefit from Judge’s sidelining. The Red Sox have a balanced lineup that can exploit any gaps in New York’s defense, and their pitching staff, anchored by veterans such as Nathan Eovaldi and emerging arms like Nick Pivetta, will aim to keep the Yankees’ offense off‑balance. The Red Sox’s manager, Alex Cora, is expected to adjust his game plan to target the Yankees’ left side of the plate, where the void left by Judge will be most palpable. Historically, teams that lose a primary power hitter in a short series often see a dip in run production, a trend the Red Sox will look to capitalize on.

Looking ahead, the Yankees’ path to the postseason will hinge on how quickly they can adapt to Judge’s absence and whether other players can step up under pressure. If New York can generate runs through a collective effort and keep the games tight, the series could still swing in their favor. However, the loss of a player who contributed more than 30 percent of the team’s home runs this year is a significant setback that will test the depth and resilience of Boone’s roster. The next few days will reveal whether the Yankees can rally without their marquee slugger or if Boston will seize the advantage and move one step closer to the American League Championship Series.
